name: First Date or Interview
blurb: One thinks it's a first date, the other a job interview, and both think it's going great
title: First Date or Interview: 2-Person Comedy Script for Actors
description: A 4-minute comedy duet for 2 adults of any gender: one thinks it is a first date, the other a job interview, and it works until it doesn't. Free to film.
h1: First Date or Interview: a 4-Minute Comedy Script for 2
logline: Robin is in a café waiting for a first date from an app. Taylor arrives to interview a candidate for an assistant job. Every question fits both situations perfectly, until a piece of paper comes out of Taylor's bag.
setting: A small café table for two, afternoon. Props: two cups, a folder with a sheet of paper, a pen, a phone.

roles.name: Robin
roles.note: 25 to 40, any gender. Nervous, hopeful, sure this is a first date. Wants to be liked.

roles.name: Taylor
roles.note: 28 to 45, any gender. Runs a tiny business alone, sure this is a job interview. Wants someone reliable, and is lonelier than they admit.

script.action: ROBIN sits at a table for two, checking their reflection in a phone screen. TAYLOR arrives with a folder and stops at the table.

script.say: Robin? Green jacket?
That's me! Hi. Wow. You look exactly like your picture.
We use the same photo on the website.
Very smart. So people know what they're getting.

script.action: They sit. Taylor opens the folder. Robin takes this as a charming quirk.

script.say: Thank you for coming. I know these things can be nerve-racking.
Honestly, I almost cancelled. But my friend said, just go, what's the worst that can happen.
Good attitude. So. Tell me about yourself.
Okay. I'm loyal. I'm a good listener. I'm told I make a very good soup.
Do you cook for others often?
I would, if there was someone to cook for.
Team player. Great. Where do you see yourself in five years?
Wow, straight in. I like that. Settled. Somewhere with a little garden. Maybe someone to come home to.
Long-term commitment. That's exactly what we're looking for. Our last person left after a month.
Oh no. What happened?
They said I was too demanding. I text a lot after hours.
I don't mind that at all. I like a good morning message.
I like a seven a.m. message.
Early riser. Noted.
Are you comfortable working late nights?
With the right person? Absolutely.
Good. Fair warning, there's a lot of ink.
Ink? Like tattoos?
On a bad day, all up your arms.
Okay. I can be open-minded.
What would you say is your biggest weakness?
I fall too fast. I give everything, right away.
Honestly, that's not a weakness here. And your last position. Why did that end?
They said they needed space. And then they moved in with their gym instructor.
Restructuring. Happens to everyone.
You are so easy to talk to.
So are you. Can I be honest? I've met six people this week and you're the first one who felt right.
Six? This week?
It's a competitive market.
Right. Well. I'm glad I made the cut.
Let's talk money.
Oh, we can split it. I don't mind.
Split it? That's very generous, but no. I pay. Every month. On the first.
Every month? You don't have to do that.
It's the law.

script.action: Taylor slides a sheet of paper and a pen across the table.

script.say: Three months' trial. Thirty-eight hours a week. If it works out, we make it permanent.

script.action: Robin stares at the paper. Picks it up very slowly.

script.say: Is this a prenup?
It's an employment contract.
For what?
For the assistant job. At my print shop. You applied on Monday.
I matched with you on Monday. On an app. You had a picture with a dog.
That's the shop dog.
You said you liked long walks!
To the post office! We do a lot of posting!

script.action: Silence. Both look around the café. Neither sees anyone else in a green jacket.

script.say: I'm so sorry. I'll go.
Wait. Are you looking for work?
I was let go in March. So, technically, yes.
And I have not been on a date in four years. So, technically, also yes.

script.action: Robin sits back down. Looks at the contract. Looks at Taylor.

script.say: Does the job come with a lunch break?
One hour. I usually spend it here.
Then I'll take the job. And you're buying lunch.
Strictly after five. I'm your boss.

script.action: Robin signs. They shake hands. Neither lets go first.

ul: All you need is a small table, two chairs and two cups. Angle the chairs slightly out so the audience sees both faces during the double meanings.
Robin is already seated and preening; Taylor enters briskly with the folder. The folder is the visual clue the audience sees before Robin does.
The contract slide is the big moment. Taylor pushes it across slowly and Robin picks it up as if it might be dangerous.
On the line about looking around the café, both actors should scan the audience as if they are the other customers.
For a self-tape, shoot across the table in a two-shot, or film it as alternating close singles with a reader. For audio, add café noise and a cup set down on each big pause.
Both characters must believe completely. The comedy dies the moment either one winks at the audience.
Robin plays warm and a little too open. Taylor plays efficient and quietly pleased. They are both having the best meeting of their week.
Give each double meaning room. The laugh comes a half second after the line, when the audience catches the second meaning, so do not jump on the next cue.
Six? This week? is the first crack. Robin should feel a tiny sting and then bravely cover it.
Play the reveal at full speed and volume; the long walks and post office exchange is a real argument. Then drop instantly into quiet for the ending.
Swap the mix-up: a flat viewing versus a first date, or a meeting with a new landlord versus a meeting with a long-lost cousin.
Add a third actor: the real date or the real job candidate who turns up in a green jacket at the very end.
Set it in a park or on a bench outside an office; the only thing that must stay is a sheet of paper that cannot be read two ways.

prompts.keyframe: Cosy café in the afternoon, an adult in a green jacket sitting nervously at a small table for two, checking their hair in a phone screen, another adult approaching with a document folder, soft daylight from a window, cinematic still, 16:9.
shots: Medium two-shot across a café table, static camera, one person talks dreamily while the other takes notes in a folder, light comic mood, warm daylight.
Close-up on a hand sliding a sheet of paper and a pen across a café table, slow push-in, the other person's face freezes in confusion.
Wide shot, both people look around the café at the same time, then back at each other, awkward comic pause, handheld gentle sway.
Close-up of two hands shaking over a signed paper on a café table, holding on a moment too long, warm hopeful mood.

faq.q: Can I film First Date or Interview for a monetised channel?
faq.a: Yes. It is an original script released under CC BY 4.0. You can perform, film and post it anywhere, including monetised channels and competitions, as long as you credit Script: cv.cm.

faq.q: How do I make the double meanings land for an audience?
faq.a: Let the audience see the folder early, so they know it is an interview before Robin does. Then every romantic answer gets a laugh, because the audience hears both versions at once.

faq.q: Can I shorten it for a 60-second video?
faq.a: Yes. Keep the opening, the five-year question, the biggest weakness, the prenup line and the last exchange. That gives you a one-minute version with the same turn and ending.
